It will be interesting to see what develops.
Until recently, personal identification has not been nearly as simple and reliable as commonly believed.
However, recently advances in science regarding DNA and obtaining and identifying and recording DNA probably could
enable a much needed means of reliable individual identification by way of a uniform nationwide registration system using DNA information for nearly all newborns for nearly all future births in the USA. Such a system could use portions of each persons human DNA which do not carry any sensitive information about such things as medical conditions or mental conditions but which which are nevertheless unique to every person to enable identification by means of DNA matches. comments.name: Kevin Blake
comments.body:
Selective memories.

The filibuster wasn't generally used for nominations to higher level courts or even the President's cabinet until 2003.  Examples include Clarence Thomas, who was confirmed 52-48 to the Supreme Court, and John Ashcroft, who was confirmed 58-42 as Attorney General.  Neither of those nominations were filibustered.  Nor was the nomination of Ted Olson to be Solicitor General, confirmed 51-47.

In 2002, Dems lost their Senate majority but believed that it was more likely than not that they would win the Presidency in 2004.  Chuck Schumer (then in his 1st term as a Senator) was the one who came up with the idea of using the filibuster to block some of then President GW Bush's nominees to the federal court.  It was a way of showing activists that they were willing to fight a lot harder against Republicans.  BTW - this was 24 years ago.  Not exactly a new sentiment in the Democrat party.

In 2003, the Dems filibustered 7 Bush nominees to the federal appeals court.  Most prominent among them was Miguel Estrada, who was widely viewed as being a potential Supreme Court nominee if he served for a year or two on the federal appeals court.

In 2005, Republicans came up with the plan to break the filibuster for nominations.  This was the first time that the term "nuclear option" was ever used.  In the end, there was an agreement to confirm 5 of the 7 nominees and to avoid breaking the filibuster.

Bottom line is that Republicans didn't start this.

I may have come full circle. Around 2000, I participated in a Columbia University light-therapy study conducted by Drs. Michael Terman and Jiuan Su Terman, using an early SAD light-therapy device. I responded well to the treatment—it helped me maintain the motivation and energy to stick to my training regimen for the 2001 marathon.

Now, 25 years later, I recognize many of my own symptoms in this article’s description of a possible circadian subtype of depression. I’m actively trying to recreate the treatment that helped me then.

Columbia’s research showed that the timing of light exposure relative to an individual’s biological clock could significantly affect treatment outcomes. This new research reinforces the promise of personalized circadian medicine: treating depression according to an individual’s biology rather than a one-size-fits-all approach.

It is unclear if Holmes still believes in her 'innovation' many years after being convicted but it seems she does in some self protective way which, of course, does not make her less culpable. 
One of the big 'elephants' in this room is the concept of self-deception. Certainly that is clear from the explanations by Holmes and Billy but also the uncertainty of the other two throughout the second half. It's a fascinating observation of real life and how humans have a significant capacity to deceive oneself and others with our self portrayal, overconfident beliefs and behaviors that attempt to portray reality to ourselves and the world. 
The film has a backdrop of trying to find truth but reveals much more about deeper human processes. I would highly recommend it as a piece to get one thinking and asking important questions. Cheers!

comments.body: What is fascinating, and puzzling, is the question of what is it that leads a young person like her down such a path in life? It seems like all children are born curious, and largely unafraid (e.g., her unhesitatingly picking up bugs), but through some events or behaviors they experience or observe, they often don’t just lose interest, they in some cases come to abhor the natural world. I ask being one of those who was similar to her at that age (although nowhere as diligent), whose path eventually led to a PhD in the sciences and a career doing science, now retired. But I cannot answer for certain, “why me”? Certainly one likely factor is the parents. Her father is a physician. Mine was a botanist, who encouraged my interest. I was allowed to keep the spider and praying mantis in my room. He drives her out to do her field work, and then doesn’t interfere. I’m willing to bet that support started way back when she was that curious, unafraid toddler. I’m sure her hand was not slapped away when she reached out for a moth on the wall. I do know that once established, the love for the natural world never ends. Just the past few evenings I was outside watching with fascination a Neoscona crucifera build her beautiful web.

Vaccines and new treatments are important, but prevention is far better.
Worldwide, 20 million people are newly diagnosed with cancer each year, and 10 million are killed by this horrible disease. If current trends continue, nearly half the population in developed countries will develop cancer during their lifetime by 2040.
What I cannot understand is why so much focus has been placed on chasing elusive cures rather than preventing cancer in the first place.
The primary driver of the relentless rise in cancer incidence over the past eight decades has been clearly identified: not genetics, not aging, not bad luck, and not even lifestyle, but cumulative exposure to toxic chemicals in our food, water, air, and consumer products.
Learn more: https://gps4health.com
Of course, we cannot avoid all toxic chemicals. However, reducing our overall exposure to safer levels is achievable. The paradigm developed by Dr. William Rea, MD, widely recognized as the father of environmental medicine, offers a practical approach to minimizing chemical exposures and maintaining health.
Rather than counting on cures, we should take action to prevent cancer from developing in the first place.

The horses are led into the sea to swim, reportedly on a daily basis. Yet the article does not address a basic question: What precautions are taken to protect these animals from the effects of repeated immersion in saltwater?

Salt residue can dry and irritate the skin, contribute to itching and flaking, and leave the coat rough and brittle. Repeated exposure may aggravate existing skin conditions, particularly if horses are not rinsed thoroughly with fresh water and allowed to dry properly. Saltwater can also irritate existing sores and complicate healing. Daily swimming does not automatically mean that horses will suffer harm, but it makes appropriate aftercare and veterinary monitoring important questions that responsible reporting should address.

Does NIHI Sumba rinse the horses after every swim? Are their skin, coats and hooves regularly examined for signs of irritation or damage? What does the resort’s veterinary team say about the long-term effects of this routine?

These are not unreasonable or trivial questions. They are fundamental to assessing whether an activity marketed as an idyllic, therapeutic experience is also being conducted in the best interests of the animals.

The financial figures quoted in the article make the omission even more troubling. Cohane reports: “Rates start at $2,053 per villa. What about those who do most of the work: the horses?

Salt residue can dry the skin, cause itching, flaking and irritation, and leave the hair rough and brittle. Repeated exposure can also aggravate existing skin conditions, particularly if the horses are not thoroughly rinsed with fresh water and allowed to dry properly after each swim. Saltwater can irritate sores and complicate healing, too. Daily swimming does not automatically mean these horses will suffer harm, but it does make proper aftercare essential. Moderna’s Cancer Vaccine: A Medical Breakthrough, but Wall Street Isn’t Impressed.

Moderna and Merck reported promising Phase 3 results for their personalized mRNA cancer vaccine, showing a 42% reduction in the relative risk of melanoma recurrence or death when combined with Keytruda.

Yet Moderna’s stock plunged as much as 25% intraday.

Think about that. A pharmaceutical company reports meaningful progress in preventing cancer from returning, and investors punish the stock because the results didn’t exceed expectations.

Of course, there are legitimate questions about manufacturing costs, insurance coverage, scalability, and whether the technology will work across other cancers. Clinical success doesn’t automatically translate into commercial success.

But here’s what concerns me: Have we become so focused on pharmaceutical profits and investor expectations that we’re losing sight of what medical innovation is supposed to accomplish?

Personalized cancer vaccines could represent a significant shift in how we treat cancer. The science is promising, even if regulatory approval and broader clinical validation are still ahead.

Ultimately, the success of this technology shouldn’t be measured by Moderna’s stock price.

It should be measured by how many patients live longer, healthier lives.

Honestly, I do not think about it too much as it is my everyday reality. However, living in a world ruled by social media and always-shifting aesthetics makes it difficult to find a balance and feel comfortable in your skin. Within an hour of scrolling down my Instagram feed, I see dozens of different styles and personas – from alternative to understated, and it is hard to decide what to aim for in the morning when heading to school. Expressing yourself in day-to-day life, as well as on social media, is more difficult than ever. One tends to face criticism online for not fitting into a certain mold or “larping” if their interests are not deemed narrow enough.
As mentioned, high school is routine, but I feel very supported by teachers and the environment around me. Speaking of environments, high school is not as cutthroat and clique-y as movies like Mean Girls or Diary of a Wimpy Kid want us to believe it is. Yes, there are popular groups of friends who are often portrayed as better than the “loser” crowd, but in reality, everyone is equal. Everyone minds their own business unless they have the urge to verbally bully someone physically or online. All in all, being a teenager is sometimes a difficult endeavor, but there is a healthy amount of support in finding your way.

comments.body:
I think being a teenager today can be challenging because teenagers have to balance school, friendships, family, and pressure from social media. In my opinion, being a teenager today can be stressful, but it is also a time to learn more about yourself and grow as a person.

One reason I think being a teenager is difficult is because of the pressure to do well in school and meet other people's expectations. Students may feel like they always have to get good grades, fit in with others, and plan for their future. Another reason is social media, because people often compare themselves to others and feel like their lives are not good enough. This can affect their confidence and mental health.

For example, students may have a lot of homework and tests while also trying to make time for their friends and family. Sometimes it can be hard to manage everything at once. I think teenagers need support from their families, teachers, and friends so they do not feel like they have to handle every problem alone.

Overall, I believe being a teenager today comes with both challenges and positive experiences. Adults should listen to teenagers and try to understand what they are going through instead of assuming that their problems are not important. Teenagers deserve to feel supported, respected, and understood.

comments.name: izabella carbajal
comments.body: Adults often say being young and a teenager is one of the best experiences of life, but it doesn't always feel like that in the moment. Why? What isn't always remembered is the stress, high expectations, and pressure to grow up. Being a teenager is always said to be easy; we just go to school, get to be social with friends, and get to do extra activities, but it's definitely more than that. We have to worry about keeping up with homework, the expectations of great grades that follow, good behavior, and making friends, while having to deal with drama, sports, what we want to do or be in the future, and most importantly, figuring out who we want to be as people. Having to balance everything while still trying to figure out what kind of person we want to be is more difficult than expected. Having so many hours of school takes up most of our days; then some have sports, and also lots of homework. And then the pressure of being social. Friendships can be good but also drama with misunderstandings. I think adults should be the most understanding because they've been through what we are currently experiencing. They were all once kids learning, trying to understand themselves, making decisions and making mistakes, like we are today. Teenagers want to be taken seriously while actually learning real responsibility and pressure and trying to become great adults. If being a teenager is this hard, I wonder how much harder being an adult is.

comments.name: Julianna Martinez
comments.body: I believe being a teenager in 2026 Is both stressful and exciting because there are so many challenges and expectations that are pressured and applied to us. One of the biggest challenges for me Is social media. As teens we constantly focus on what it is to be considered as "accepted" in today's society. Whether it comes to trends or clothes or simply posting a picture, I often find myself with second thoughts and begin to compare myself to others. We see people online who seem to have perfect lives and sometimes forget that social media does not show everything. Another challenge we often face is the pressure to succeed. Many students worry about grades, college and their futures. As a junior in high school I understand the difficulty of balancing all these responsibilities and still having the ability to make time for yourself. Teens should be able to enjoy their youth instead of constantly worrying about what might come next.

comments.name: Lizeth
comments.body: I think that as teenagers now, we are easily influenced by social media trends or styles and we are in a time where a lot of information is edited or unattainable. Constant peer pressure to fit into a certain category or label is what I think a lot of people my age fall to, including myself at times. However, being a teenager really isn't that bad, we get to try out for sports teams, be involved in communities, free lunch, and overall we don't really have many responsibilities. We still have the privilege of being able to figure out what we want to do in life and explore ourselves as people. I think that being as a teenager, perspective either makes or breaks these years of life.

comments.name: Itzel Leon-Soltero
comments.body: What's it like being a teenager right now? It depends on the situation and different perspectives of everyone because everyone has different things going on in their lives. Some may be struggling some may be striving, others are busy others arent. Many stereotypes go on saying teenagers are hormonal and only want to have fun and not focus on their academics. I dont think that ´s the case, me for example I have marching band practice daily throughout the week so I have to balance that AND school. But that is just me, others may not take school seriously and others will, it depends on the perspective you see from that teenager.

comments.name: Jayda Banuelos
comments.body: Being a teenager right now I feel like it is honestly a really fun time. I am in my opinion at the perfect age group of my teenager life. Social media is a big thing, and although some say that it harms kids, I find social media to be a good thing like sharing photos, calling and texting friends, posting fun, watching videos of others, and so much more! These teenage years have also definitely taught me a lot in the last 2 years and have shaped me as a person and changed the way I will view things for the rest of my life. School can be extremely stressful especially with a sport. I play varsity basketball, and with my season quickly approaching especially during winter and final season it can be hard. It's taught me how to manage my schedule and time without draining myself too much. Overall, being a teenager right now shapes me in a lot of different positive ways, and I enjoy being a teenager in this time period a lot!

comments.name: Victoria De Leon
comments.body: To be a teenager right now, for me at least, is kind of confusing but also the most fun I've had in my not so long life. Although many people glorify and romanticize being a teen during 2014 or 2016 I don't think I've would want to be a teen any other time than now. Im grateful to be able to say that I love being a teenager currently. Right now my life as a teen looks like cheering at Friday night football games and ending up at In-N-Out after every game no matter how tired i get of it, because everyone knows that In-N-Out is just where you have to be after a game. As immature as it sounds I find it amusing watching all the ways my friends try to work around the new cellphone bans at my school. I appreciate how people my age express themselves and seeing the different styles girls have at my school, I love complimenting other girls outfits in the hallways. I like laughing at my chronically online friends when they make odd "niche" references to some sort of piece of media. I appreciate how most pre my age are addicted to Starbucks, i like when people recommend me new drinks. I love being a teenager right now.

comments.name: EB
comments.body:
This story highlights just how vital social trust is to public health. In eastern Congo there are decades and decades of reasons to not trust the government, and not much of a reason to trust the NGOs that pop in when an outbreak occurs. But the church has deep ties to the community, and can be the tool that opens people's ears and minds.
Ebola seems particularly cruel to me. The people who show the greatest level of care to the sick are the ones who fall ill. It's not a random breath of contaminated air like measles, but the close contact of a person who is trying to live out their empathy and support of others. Family, medical workers, and those honoring the dead are at particular risk. It breaks my heart that hugging an ailing child becomes a death sentence with ebola. 
The people in this region have suffered so much for so long. It is absolutely wonderful to see survivers of ebola going out and saving others.

comments.name: Faizyab
comments.body: Honestly? Only if the narrator commits to the bit. Footage of me debugging a Python program at 1 a.m. is unbearably boring, forty minutes of stillness, one error message, a boy staring until a David Attenborough voice says, "The subject has not moved. The error remains undefeated." Suddenly it's riveting. My life has no plot, just a loop of school, code, and meals, which is exactly what a good documentary needs: small things taken seriously. I'd include the midnight coding scene, narrated like a nature documentary about a nocturnal mammal. Why or why not? Why not - I'm already narrating my own life in my head anyway; I'd just be letting the camera in on it.

comments.name: Donovan Castillo
comments.body: My life would make an amazing documentary, from relationship struggles, to terrible haircuts, my life has been fairly tumultuous. I also go to a ton of local shows, and tons of stuff goes on there, so that would also make it a fair bit more interesting. The show could maybe document how I have changed as a person, showing how my music taste has shifted, or how my style has changed and evolved. Last but definitely not least, they could document my rocky love life, maybe even interviewing those ive talked to and dated in the past to glean what exactly makes it so edifficult for me to get along with some. They could also analyze why even after having my heart broken by the same person twice, I would still take an opportunity with her if it presented itself.

I think people who make these mockumentaries are just trying to have fun and making other people laugh with them. I think yes, Stephon Crawford does resonate with my thinking because it’s just displaying your work life or home life, and a second source of income. This kind of relationship is very healthy because people are just trying to document their lives, and maybe they’ll become famous one day.

Cats are very good at emotional connection and their purring is very healing and soothing, so yes, people are using both dogs and cats for emotional companionship. Dogs do require more training and should be walked. Cats never lose their survival skills, they are apex predators. Most could survive without their owners, no question. Cats are social, they are just not pack animals whereas dogs and humans are. 
I suspect we will be switching to robots soon enough for that emotional connection and companionship. I think most humans have lost their capacity for intimacy, if indeed, we ever had it, but we do crave emotional connection. And robots would require less care and not be so messy.
